transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-12-18 15:00 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lina Ortiz (Redwood CSM); Aisha Rahman (StratusScale Lead ML Eng), Mark Thompson (PM), Diego Alvarez (SRE), Priya Sharma (Data Eng), Ella (note taker)

Auto-generated summary (may be incomplete): Quick sync on coalescing change rolled last week, observed +7% KV hit overall but 85th/95th latency increased for some request patterns, discuss rolling back vs tuning prefetch.

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, we got like 42 minutes, so we'll go through the key metrics and then actions. Samir, do you want to share the chart?
[00:14] Samir Patel: Yup, sharing screen now, umm, sorry the dashboard link is in the chat - it's the coalesce-playbook metrics. so first slide, total KV hit up 7 percent week over week, prefix reuse increased about 12 percent.
[00:30] Aisha Rahman: quick clarifying q, when you say prefix reuse is that dedup of identical prompt prefixes or heuristics that fuzzy match?
[00:40] Samir Patel: Good q. Right now it's exact prefix hash + a small levenshtein fallback at 0.85 similarity, so most of the bump came from exact matches of onboarding flows.
[00:55] Mark Thompson: We did expand the user flow on Dec 10 so that makes sense. But we saw some odd latency.
[01:05] Diego Alvarez: yeah the 95th went from 310ms to 520ms in the evening window, so tail spiked. We traced to a coalescing path where multiple large prompts attempted to be batched and KV lookups got serialized.
[01:22] Samir Patel: Right, that's the coalescing + prefetch interaction. When the coalesce window is too wide, you get more cache hits but you also increase contention on the KV retrieval which can push tail latency up if prefetching isn't throttled.
[01:38] Aisha Rahman: there's also a pattern where the model re-generates for some prompts, the prefix gets evicted and then comes back — I think our workload has a lot of mid-length sequences that cause eviction churn.
[01:52] Jordan Lee: Yeah eviction churn is common with mid-length sequences. Two knobs we discussed: shrink the coalescing window (less batching but lower contention) or tune prefetch throttle — only prefetch on hot keys above a hit-prob threshold.
[02:08] Priya Sharma: Can we get a quick breakdown by cohort? Our mobile clients vs web behave differently.
[02:15] Samir Patel: We have split cohorts on the dashboard. Mobile flows have higher repetition so better gains from coalescing. Web flows show more unique tokens. I'll paste cohort CSV after the call.
[02:30] Mark Thompson: also curious about prompt reuse heuristics. Right now we are exact matching prefixes; could fuzzy matching reduce misses but increase false positives?
[02:40] Samir Patel: Exact match is safer for correctness. Fuzzy raises chance of returning slightly off-context cache hits — you saw that in the last regen rates. We can do a hybrid: exact match for top N keys and fuzzy for long tail.
[02:55] Aisha Rahman: what about the prefetch threshold? currently it's at 0.6 predicted hit probability.
[03:02] Samir Patel: Yes. We can raise to 0.75 for evening windows or implement an adaptive threshold that steps up as observed hit rate increases. But that reduces prefetch volume and might reduce overall hit gains.
[03:18] Diego Alvarez: the main worry is the disk-bound KV store. If too many prefetches arrive concurrently during peak, I/O saturates and latency goes up. Did you measure I/O queue depth?
[03:27] Samir Patel: We did a short capture. Queue_depth spiked with the wider window, that's in the perf trace Samir uploaded.
[03:33] Jordan Lee: Ok logistically we proposed a couple experiments: A) shrink coalescing window from 4s->2s but enable aggressive prefetch for top 10% keys; B) keep window at 4s but cap prefetch concurrency to 12 and raise hit prob to 0.75; C) enable hybrid fuzzy matching only for requests with high context similarity. We'll pick two to replay.
[03:54] Aisha Rahman: I'd vote for B and C, because shrinking window might drop too much benefit for mobile, which we care about.
[04:02] Priya Sharma: Agreed, mobile performance is critical.
[04:06] Mark Thompson: B + C sounds good. Also can we add an alert for eviction churn rate? If eviction rate > X per minute, rollback the coalesce widen.
[04:16] Lina Ortiz: We can add that in Ops runbook and CloudWatch Alert; I'll draft the threshold proposal.
[04:24] Jordan Lee: Samir, can you walk through the replay plan?
[04:28] Samir Patel: Sure. We'll replay the last 48 hours of traffic in staging with config B then C. Replay uses the same traffic shape but with non-prod model to avoid cost. We'll capture KV hit, tail latencies, I/O queue depth, and regen rate. Expected runtime ~6 hours for full replay but we can do a sliced 4-hour window for quicker feedback.
[04:50] Diego Alvarez: How do we simulate spikes? Our evenings have traffic bursts.
[04:54] Samir Patel: We have a burst replay script that overlays the evening pattern. We'll run that as part of the test.
[05:00] Aisha Rahman: Any risk to data privacy in replay? We need redaction.
[05:04] Jordan Lee: We'll use tokenized/hashed keys and synthetic prompt bodies. We won't store any PII. Lina will share the redaction checklist.
[05:12] Mark Thompson: On security, we still need the KMS integration docs and an expected timeline for on-prem option if we decide to move.
[05:19] Lina Ortiz: I'll send SOC2 and KMS integration notes today. Private deployment estimate requires a separate scoping but we can start that if you want.
[05:28] Priya Sharma: We might need on-prem for EU customers next quarter, so please include a ballpark in the doc.
[05:34] Jordan Lee: Noted. Samir, any preliminary numbers on cost savings vs cost of prefetch I/O?
[05:40] Samir Patel: Preliminary spreadsheet shows approx 18-24% token cost reduction assuming current load and a stable 7-10% KV hit. But if prefetch increases I/O, backend costs rise. We'll attach a more detailed cost model.
[05:54] Aisha Rahman: One oddity — we saw a class of requests with very long prompt prefixes that churn the KV size and cause eviction. Any way to cap prefix length for caching?
[06:05] Samir Patel: Yes you can set a max-prefix window and also normalize long prefixes (hash suffix). That avoids storing huge entries. We recommend max 512 tokens or a sliding window.
[06:16] Diego Alvarez: If we normalize, do we risk cache poisoning or mismatches?
[06:20] Samir Patel: There's always a tradeoff. Normalization reduces cardinality but might increase false hits. We suggested normalization only for very long prefixes.
[06:30] Mark Thompson: Could we instrument a canary that normalizes for 5% of traffic?
[06:33] Jordan Lee: Yep canary is straightforward — route 5% to a normalized prefix path and compare. Add that to action items.
[06:42] Aisha Rahman: For the bench run next week, we want kernel-level traces to see where the serialization occurs. Samir you mentioned a kernel trace.
[06:48] Samir Patel: I'll run a 30-minute bench with perf counters and nvprof on the inference nodes, capture the exact moments of KV serialization, and correlate with I/O.
[06:56] Priya Sharma: please also capture CPU steal and GC pauses on the KV side — those can hide as tail latency.
[07:02] Samir Patel: Will do.
[07:05] Jordan Lee: Ok quick recap of agreed experiments: run replay with config B (cap prefetch concurrency + raise threshold) and config C (hybrid fuzzy on long-tail); run a 5% canary with prefix normalization; run bench for kernel trace next Tue. Action owners are on the list.
[07:24] Ella (note taker): Noted actions: Jordan send configs; Aisha run replay; Diego validate eviction; Samir bench prep; Lina SOC2 docs.
[07:34] Aisha Rahman: timeline question — if replay shows worse tail, what's rollback plan?
[07:38] Jordan Lee: We'll revert coalescing change in prod via a single toggle and use the short rollback runbook, should be under 15 minutes to revert traffic to previous config. We'll test rollback in staging as part of the replay.
[07:51] Mark Thompson: ok last Q — do we have a recommended default for prefetch concurrency? You mentioned 12 earlier. Is that per-node?
[07:57] Samir Patel: Yes 12 per-kv-node is conservative. We can scale with node count; initial cap 12 is safe for your current cluster size.
[08:06] Diego Alvarez: fine. We'll start with 12 and monitor queue depth.
[08:10] Jordan Lee: Great. Any final questions?
[08:14] Priya Sharma: none from me.
[08:16] Aisha Rahman: no.
[08:18] Jordan Lee: Awesome, we'll follow up with the spreadsheets and configs. Thanks everyone.
